trunkFlex:-.note: Bending forward from standing is controlled by the same extensors working eccentrically; gravity provides the flexion.

trunkLat:+.note: Side bending to the right uses the right-side muscles shown in the model.

trunkLat:-.note: Side bending to the left uses the same muscles on the left side (the mirror image of the right side in the model).

trunkRot:+.note: Rotation to the right pairs the right internal oblique with the left external oblique, helped by the left-side multifidus and rotatores.

trunkRot:-.note: Rotation to the left pairs the right external oblique with the left internal oblique. The right-side transversospinales also turn the spine to the left.

neckFlex:+.note: Lifting the head off a pillow starts with the deep flexors (longus colli and capitis) tucking the chin; sternocleidomastoid then flexes the neck.

neckRot:+.note: Turning to the right also uses the left sternocleidomastoid. Most rotation happens at the atlanto-axial joint (C1–C2).

neckRot:-.note: Turning to the left also uses the left splenius capitis and the left suboccipital muscles.

shoulderFlex:+.note: Above about 90° the scapula must rotate upward (trapezius and serratus anterior). The model moves only the humerus.

shoulderFlex:-.note: The sternocostal head of pectoralis major extends the shoulder only from a flexed position.

shoulderAbd:+.note: Supraspinatus starts the movement and keeps the humeral head seated while deltoid lifts. Beyond about 90° the scapula rotates upward (trapezius and serratus anterior: the scapulohumeral rhythm). The model moves only the humerus.

shoulderRot:+.note: Medial rotators far outnumber lateral rotators, which is one reason the shoulder rests in medial rotation after injury.

elbowFlex:+.note: Brachialis works in every forearm position; biceps is strongest with the forearm supinated, brachioradialis with it half-way.

forearmPro:+.note: Pronator quadratus starts pronation; pronator teres adds power, especially against resistance. Brachioradialis only brings the forearm back to mid-position.

forearmPro:-.note: Supinator works alone in slow or unresisted supination with the elbow straight; biceps joins in when the elbow is bent and there is resistance (turning a screwdriver).

wristFlex:-.note: The wrist extensors also stabilise the wrist in slight extension during every power grip.

wristDev:+.note: Ulnar deviation pairs a flexor and an extensor so their flexion and extension cancel out.

hipFlex:-.note: In normal walking the hamstrings do most of the work; gluteus maximus takes over for forceful extension such as climbing or rising from a chair.

hipAbd:+.note: Their most important job is keeping the pelvis level when the opposite foot is off the ground.

knee:-.note: Tensor fasciae latae steadies the extended knee through the iliotibial tract rather than extending it.

scapular-upward-rotation.name: Upward rotation of the scapula
scapular-upward-rotation.note: Needed for the arm to go overhead. Upper trapezius pulls the acromion up, lower trapezius pulls the medial spine down, and the lower serratus pulls the inferior angle forward: a force couple.

neck-lateral-flexion.name: Lateral flexion of the neck (to the right)

jaw-depression.name: Opening the jaw (depression)
jaw-depression.note: Gravity does much of the work; lateral pterygoid pulls the condyle forward so the jaw can open wide.

jaw-retraction.name: Jaw retraction
jaw-retraction.note: The horizontal back fibres of temporalis do this.

jaw-side-to-side.name: Side-to-side grinding
jaw-side-to-side.note: Moving the jaw to the left uses the right pterygoids with the left temporalis, and the reverse.

quiet-inspiration.name: Quiet breathing in
quiet-inspiration.note: Quiet breathing out is passive: the lungs and chest wall recoil.

forced-inspiration.name: Forced breathing in
forced-inspiration.note: The accessory muscles of respiration (sternocleidomastoid, scalenes, pectoralis minor) are visibly active in people in respiratory distress.

forced-expiration.name: Forced breathing out
forced-expiration.note: The abdominal muscles push the abdominal contents up against the diaphragm, as in coughing.

abdominal-compression.name: Raising abdominal pressure
abdominal-compression.note: Used in coughing, lifting, defecation and childbirth, with the diaphragm and pelvic floor closing the top and bottom of the cylinder.

finger-flexion.name: Finger flexion
finger-flexion.note: Profundus bends the fingertips (DIP), superficialis the middle joints (PIP); lumbricals and interossei bend the knuckles (MCP).

finger-extension.name: Finger extension
finger-extension.note: Extensor digitorum mainly extends the knuckles; the lumbricals and interossei extend the finger joints beyond them.

foot-inversion.name: Inversion
foot-inversion.note: Happens mainly at the subtalar and transverse tarsal joints, not the ankle.

tibial-medial-rotation.name: Medial rotation of the tibia
tibial-medial-rotation.note: Not animated yet. Only possible with the knee bent.

tibial-lateral-rotation.name: Lateral rotation of the tibia
tibial-lateral-rotation.note: Not animated yet. Only possible with the knee bent.

knee-unlocking.name: Unlocking the extended knee
knee-unlocking.note: Popliteus rotates the femur laterally on the planted tibia to start flexion from full extension. The rotation itself is not animated yet.

tongue-retraction.name: Pulling the tongue down and back

femoral.name: Femoral nerve
femoral.injury: Weak knee extension, so the knee buckles on stairs or slopes; weak hip flexion; reduced or absent patellar reflex; numbness over the front of the thigh and medial leg.
femoral.note: Lumbar plexus. Enters the thigh under the inguinal ligament, lateral to the femoral artery.

obturator.name: Obturator nerve
obturator.injury: Weak hip adduction, so the leg swings outward when walking; numbness over the medial thigh.
obturator.note: Lumbar plexus. Leaves the pelvis through the obturator foramen.

lumbar-plexus-direct.name: Direct branches of the lumbar plexus
lumbar-plexus-direct.injury: Rarely injured alone; lumbar root problems weaken psoas and quadratus lumborum together with the other lumbar-supplied muscles.
lumbar-plexus-direct.note: Short branches straight from the anterior rami to psoas, quadratus lumborum and the intertransversarii.

superior-gluteal.name: Superior gluteal nerve
superior-gluteal.injury: Weak hip abduction: when standing on the affected leg the pelvis drops on the other side (positive Trendelenburg sign), giving a waddling or lurching gait.
superior-gluteal.note: Sacral plexus. Leaves the pelvis above piriformis. Can be injured by a badly placed gluteal injection.

inferior-gluteal.name: Inferior gluteal nerve
inferior-gluteal.injury: Weak hip extension: difficulty rising from a chair, climbing stairs or jumping; the trunk lurches backward at heel strike.
inferior-gluteal.note: Sacral plexus. Leaves the pelvis below piriformis and supplies only gluteus maximus.

nerve-to-piriformis.name: Nerve to piriformis
nerve-to-piriformis.injury: Isolated injury is rare and of little functional consequence.

nerve-to-obturator-internus.name: Nerve to obturator internus
nerve-to-obturator-internus.injury: Isolated injury is rare; weak lateral rotation is masked by the other rotators.
nerve-to-obturator-internus.note: Sacral plexus. Also supplies superior gemellus.

nerve-to-quadratus-femoris.name: Nerve to quadratus femoris
nerve-to-quadratus-femoris.injury: Isolated injury is rare; weak lateral rotation is masked by the other rotators.
nerve-to-quadratus-femoris.note: Sacral plexus. Also supplies inferior gemellus.

sciatic.name: Sciatic nerve
sciatic.injury: Weak knee flexion and hip extension from loss of the hamstrings, and loss of every muscle below the knee: foot drop and inability to stand on the toes.
sciatic.note: The largest nerve in the body. Two divisions in one sheath (tibial and common fibular) that usually separate above the knee.

tibial.name: Tibial nerve
tibial.injury: In the thigh (tibial division): weak hamstrings. Below the knee: weak plantarflexion and toe flexion, so push-off fails and the person cannot rise onto the toes; numb sole.
tibial.note: Continues behind the medial malleolus into the foot as the medial and lateral plantar nerves.

common-fibular.name: Common fibular nerve
common-fibular.injury: Foot drop: the foot cannot be dorsiflexed or everted and the toes cannot be extended, giving a high-stepping or slapping gait; numbness of the lateral leg and dorsum of the foot.
common-fibular.note: Wraps around the neck of the fibula, where it is the most frequently injured nerve of the lower limb (fractures, tight casts, crossed legs).

deep-fibular.name: Deep fibular nerve
atlas: Muscular branches of deep fibular nerve
deep-fibular.injury: Foot drop and weak toe extension; numbness only in the web space between the first and second toes.
deep-fibular.note: Supplies the anterior compartment of the leg and the dorsum of the foot.

superficial-fibular.name: Superficial fibular nerve
superficial-fibular.injury: Weak eversion (the foot tends to invert, risking ankle sprains); numbness over most of the dorsum of the foot.
superficial-fibular.note: Supplies the lateral compartment of the leg.

medial-plantar.name: Medial plantar nerve
medial-plantar.injury: Weak big-toe flexion and abduction; numbness over the medial sole.
medial-plantar.note: Supplies abductor hallucis, flexor digitorum brevis, flexor hallucis brevis and the first lumbrical.

lateral-plantar.name: Lateral plantar nerve
lateral-plantar.injury: Weak intrinsic foot muscles, with clawing of the lateral toes; numbness of the lateral sole.
lateral-plantar.note: Supplies most of the intrinsic muscles of the sole.

axillary.name: Axillary nerve
axillary.injury: Weak shoulder abduction beyond the first few degrees, with a flattened deltoid; numbness over the lower deltoid (the regimental badge area).
axillary.note: Posterior cord of the brachial plexus. Winds around the surgical neck of the humerus, where fractures and dislocations injure it.

suprascapular.name: Suprascapular nerve
suprascapular.injury: Weak initiation of abduction and weak lateral rotation, with wasting above and below the spine of the scapula.
suprascapular.note: Upper trunk of the brachial plexus. Passes through the suprascapular notch.

subscapular.name: Upper and lower subscapular nerves
subscapular.injury: Weak medial rotation of the shoulder.
subscapular.note: Posterior cord of the brachial plexus.

lower-subscapular.name: Lower subscapular nerve
lower-subscapular.injury: Weak medial rotation and adduction of the shoulder.
lower-subscapular.note: Supplies teres major and the lower part of subscapularis.

thoracodorsal.name: Thoracodorsal nerve
thoracodorsal.injury: Weak shoulder extension and adduction: difficulty with climbing, crutch walking and pushing up from a chair.
thoracodorsal.note: Posterior cord of the brachial plexus.

musculocutaneous.name: Musculocutaneous nerve
musculocutaneous.injury: Weak elbow flexion and supination (brachioradialis still flexes the elbow); reduced biceps reflex; numbness along the lateral forearm.
musculocutaneous.note: Lateral cord of the brachial plexus. Pierces coracobrachialis.

radial.name: Radial nerve
radial.injury: Above the elbow (for example a mid-shaft humerus fracture): wrist drop, with no extension of the wrist, fingers or thumb; triceps usually spared because its branches leave higher up. Numbness over the back of the hand near the thumb.
radial.note: Posterior cord of the brachial plexus. Runs in the radial groove of the humerus.

posterior-interosseous.name: Posterior interosseous nerve (deep branch of radial)
posterior-interosseous.injury: Finger and thumb drop with the wrist still able to extend (extensor carpi radialis longus is spared), deviating toward the radial side. No sensory loss.
posterior-interosseous.note: Passes through supinator, where it can be compressed.

median.name: Median nerve
median.injury: At the wrist (carpal tunnel syndrome): weak, wasted thenar muscles, poor opposition, and numbness of the thumb, index, middle and half the ring finger. At the elbow: also weak pronation, wrist flexion and index and middle finger flexion (the 'hand of benediction' when making a fist).
median.note: Lateral and medial cords of the brachial plexus.

anterior-interosseous.name: Anterior interosseous nerve
anterior-interosseous.injury: Cannot make an 'OK' sign: the tips of the thumb and index finger cannot bend. Weak pronation with the elbow bent. No sensory loss.
anterior-interosseous.note: A purely motor branch of the median nerve in the forearm.

ulnar.name: Ulnar nerve
ulnar.injury: Clawing of the ring and little fingers, wasted interossei, weak finger spreading and closing, a positive Froment's sign (weak adductor pollicis), and numbness of the little finger and half the ring finger.
ulnar.note: Medial cord of the brachial plexus. Exposed behind the medial epicondyle (the funny bone) and in the cubital tunnel.

accessory.name: Accessory nerve (XI)
accessory.injury: Weak shoulder shrug and difficulty raising the arm overhead, a drooping shoulder, and weak head turning to the opposite side.
accessory.note: Crosses the posterior triangle of the neck superficially, where it can be cut in lymph node surgery.

dorsal-scapular.name: Dorsal scapular nerve
dorsal-scapular.injury: Weak scapular retraction; the medial border of the scapula may drift away from the spine.
dorsal-scapular.note: Directly from the C5 root of the brachial plexus.

long-thoracic.name: Long thoracic nerve
long-thoracic.injury: Winged scapula: the medial border lifts off the chest wall when pushing forward, and raising the arm overhead is difficult.
long-thoracic.note: Directly from the C5–C7 roots; runs on the outer surface of serratus anterior, exposed in the axilla.

lateral-pectoral.name: Lateral pectoral nerve
lateral-pectoral.injury: Weak shoulder adduction and medial rotation (mainly the clavicular head of pectoralis major).
lateral-pectoral.note: Lateral cord of the brachial plexus.

medial-pectoral.name: Medial pectoral nerve
medial-pectoral.injury: Weak pectoralis minor and sternocostal pectoralis major.
medial-pectoral.note: Medial cord of the brachial plexus. Named for its cord, so it lies lateral to the lateral pectoral nerve.

nerve-to-subclavius.name: Nerve to subclavius
nerve-to-subclavius.note: Upper trunk of the brachial plexus.

phrenic.name: Phrenic nerve
phrenic.injury: Paralysis of half the diaphragm, which rises on that side; breathlessness when lying down or exercising.
phrenic.note: Runs down over scalenus anterior. Its C3–C5 origin is why high cervical cord injuries stop breathing.

intercostal.name: Intercostal nerves
intercostal.injury: Segmental weakness of the chest wall and a band of numbness around the chest (as in shingles, which follows one nerve).
intercostal.note: Anterior rami of T1–T11, running in the groove under each rib.

thoracoabdominal.name: Thoracoabdominal nerves
thoracoabdominal.injury: Weakness or bulging of part of the abdominal wall and a band of numbness on the abdomen.
thoracoabdominal.note: The lower intercostal nerves (T7–T11) continuing into the abdominal wall. T10 supplies the skin at the umbilicus.

subcostal.name: Subcostal nerve
subcostal.injury: Weakness of the lowest part of the abdominal wall.
subcostal.note: Anterior ramus of T12, running below the twelfth rib.

posterior-rami.name: Posterior rami of spinal nerves
posterior-rami.injury: Segmental weakness of the deep back muscles and numbness over the back next to the spine.
posterior-rami.note: Every true (deep) back muscle is supplied by posterior rami, one of the features that defines them.

suboccipital.name: Suboccipital nerve
suboccipital.injury: Rarely injured; weak fine control of head position.
suboccipital.note: Posterior ramus of C1. Purely motor.

nerve-to-levator-ani.name: Nerve to levator ani
nerve-to-levator-ani.injury: Weak pelvic floor: urinary and faecal incontinence and pelvic organ prolapse. Often stretched during childbirth.
nerve-to-levator-ani.note: Branches of the anterior rami of S3–S4 (with contributions from the pudendal nerve).

facial.name: Facial nerve (VII)
facial.injury: Facial palsy on that side: cannot raise the eyebrow, close the eye or smile evenly; the mouth droops. A forehead that still moves suggests a stroke rather than a nerve lesion.
facial.note: Five branches in the face: temporal, zygomatic, buccal, marginal mandibular and cervical.

trigeminal-mandibular.name: Trigeminal nerve, mandibular division (V3)
trigeminal-mandibular.injury: Weak chewing on that side; the jaw deviates toward the weak side on opening; numbness of the lower face and chin.
trigeminal-mandibular.note: The only division of the trigeminal nerve with motor fibres.

abducens.name: Abducens nerve (VI)
abducens.injury: The eye cannot turn outward; double vision when looking to that side.

trochlear.name: Trochlear nerve (IV)
trochlear.injury: Vertical double vision, worst when looking down and inward (reading, going downstairs); the head tilts away from the affected side.

hypoglossal.name: Hypoglossal nerve (XII)
hypoglossal.injury: The protruded tongue deviates toward the weak side, which wastes over time; speech and swallowing are affected.
hypoglossal.note: Supplies all tongue muscles except palatoglossus.

c1-via-hypoglossal.name: C1 fibres carried by the hypoglossal nerve
c1-via-hypoglossal.note: Spinal nerve fibres that hitch a ride with CN XII to reach geniohyoid and thyrohyoid.

ansa-cervicalis.name: Ansa cervicalis
ansa-cervicalis.injury: Weak infrahyoid muscles; usually little noticeable effect.
ansa-cervicalis.note: A loop from the cervical plexus lying on the carotid sheath.

cervical-anterior-rami.name: Anterior rami of cervical nerves
cervical-anterior-rami.injury: Segmental weakness of the deep neck flexors and scalenes, as with cervical root compression.
cervical-anterior-rami.note: Short direct branches to the prevertebral muscles and scalenes.
